Peekaboo is the first joke: most babies enjoy hide-and-reveal from about 1 month, and half produce humour of their own by 11 months.
Wrong-name jokes fit from about 29 months and nonsense knock-knocks from about 37 months, when three-quarters of children reach them.
Keep it never scary: babies are likelier to cry when a stranger plays peekaboo, so a familiar face and a soft 'boo' matter more than the line.

faqs.question: At what age does a baby first get a joke?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most parents expect. In Mireault's 2017 home studies, 5-month-olds laughed at absurd events such as a ball worn as a clown nose even when their parents stayed straight-faced, and the Early Humor Survey reports half of children producing humour of their own by 11 months.

faqs.question: Can a 2-year-old tell a knock-knock joke?
faqs.answer: Usually only as a game of sounds. The Early Humor Survey places nonsense knock-knocks in its 'playing with concepts' item, reached by three-quarters of children at 37 months, and real puns stayed rare up to 47 months. Let a 2-year-old shout 'who's there?' and give the answer yourself.

faqs.question: Is peekaboo really a kind of joke?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Early Humor Survey lists hide-and-reveal games as a humour type, and it is the earliest one, enjoyed by most babies from about 1 month. A sheet-ghost version is simply peekaboo dressed for Halloween.

faqs.question: Why does my toddler want the same joke again and again?
faqs.answer: At this age the reveal is the joke, and knowing it is coming is part of the fun. Repeat it until the laughter fades, then change one detail, such as a new wrong name, rather than starting a new joke.

faqs.question: Are ghost jokes too scary for a 1-year-old?
faqs.answer: Not if a familiar adult tells them gently. Use a sheet or your hands rather than a mask, keep 'boo' at talking volume and say 'it's me' straight after. The survey's authors cite work showing babies are likelier to cry when a stranger plays peekaboo than when a parent does.

faqs.question: What should I do if my toddler cries during a Halloween joke?
faqs.answer: Stop, show your face and name yourself, then go back to a joke that already made them laugh. Leave the spooky ones for another day; plain peekaboo works in any month.

faqs.question: How do I make up my own Halloween joke for a toddler?
faqs.answer: Pick a Halloween object and give it the wrong name, the wrong sound or a silly action: a pumpkin called a banana, a bat that moos. Mislabelling jokes suit children from about 29 months, when half of children in the survey appreciated them.

faqs.question: Do toddlers in other countries laugh at the same things?
faqs.answer: Across the four countries the Early Humor Survey sampled, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, it found no country differences in early humour. Those are all English-speaking samples, so it says nothing yet about other languages.

faqs.question: Can I send my toddler's Halloween joke to a grandparent?
faqs.answer: Yes. The /happy-halloween card has a spooky-cute kids tone and holds up to six photos and a letter, so a costume photo and the favourite joke fit. The premium page adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds if you want the joke in your toddler's own voice.

faqs.question: Do these jokes work at a toddler Halloween party?
faqs.answer: The peekaboo, action and finish-the-rhyme jokes work well with a small group, because every child can shout an answer. The SubhSandesh Halloween page is not a party tool, though; it is a greeting for one person.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Jokes for Toddlers: 46 Silly Lines for Ages 1 to 4

Halloween jokes for toddlers work when the funny part is something a child can see or hear go wrong: a pumpkin called a banana, a ghost that sneezes, a sheet hiding your face. Wordplay comes much later; in a 2021 survey covering 671 children aged 1 to 47 months, fewer than one in four had come to enjoy puns by 47 months.

Many end up on a grandparent's screen: across SubhSandesh, 48.4% of page views are on a touch device and each page averages 11.1 views (all page types, not Halloween data). Below are 46 original jokes in six types, a month-by-month table and a never-scary rule.

## What is a toddler Halloween joke?

A toddler joke is a small, harmless surprise a trusted adult sets up and reveals: a hidden face, a wrong name, a silly noise. It needs no punchline, because the mismatch itself is funny.

The [Early Humor Survey by Elena Hoicka and colleagues](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9374637), in Behavior Research Methods (November 2021), charts it month by month. Half of children were reported to produce humour by 11 months and 97.5% by 25 months, with no differences between the Australian, Canadian, British and American families sampled.

## Why do toddlers laugh at mistakes instead of wordplay?

Toddlers laugh at incongruity, something that breaks what they expect, years before they can untangle a double meaning. In [two longitudinal studies of 113 babies in the British Journal of Developmental Psychology (2017)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6171116), Gina Mireault's team showed absurd events, such as a ball worn as a clown nose. Five-month-olds laughed even when their parents kept a straight face.

A [2020 paper in Human Development](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8291289) draws the line between funny and frightening. Humorous incongruity is odd but possible, harmless and nonthreatening, while a physically impossible event tends to make babies stare rather than smile.

Familiar adults matter too. A [2025 Developmental Psychobiology study](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12464472) of 35 five-month-olds linked more smiling and laughter in everyday play with caregivers to stronger connectivity in one brain network, an association rather than proof.

## 46 Halloween jokes for toddlers, by joke type

Each type gives the age, what to do, then the lines. Pause before every reveal and repeat what lands.

### 1. Peekaboo ghost games

Hide-and-reveal is the earliest humour on the Early Humor Survey, enjoyed by most babies from about 1 month. Use a muslin as the ghost sheet, never a mask, and reveal smiling.

- Cloth over your face: "Is there a ghost in here? Peekaboo, it's only me!"
- Cloth over a toy pumpkin: "Where did Pumpkin roll to? Pop, there it is!"
- Child under a blanket: "A ghost on the sofa! Hang on, ghosts don't have wiggly toes."
- Hands over your eyes: "Ghost eyes shut... ghost eyes WIDE open!"
- Bat puppet behind your back: "Flap, flap, where's Batty? Peep, here's Batty!"
- Sock in the treat bucket: "What's inside? A sweet? No, a stinky sock!"
- Behind the curtain: "One, two, three... a smiley ghost!"
- Swap roles: "Your turn to be the ghost. Is it under the cushion? Is it YOU?"

### 2. Silly-sound jokes

Half of babies enjoyed funny voices by 1 month and three-quarters by 17 months, so this set suits 12 to 24 months. Make each sound bigger than feels natural, then wait.

- The ghost has a cold: "Ah... ah... ah-BOO!"
- The black cat sees a pumpkin pie: "Mee-YUM!"
- The witch's broom has hiccups: "Swish-HIC, swish-HIC!"
- The skeleton bumped its knee: "Rattle, rattle, BONK!"
- The pumpkin ate its supper: "BLUUURP-kin!"
- The tiny spider tiptoes up an arm: "Tippy, tippy, tap... TICKLE!"
- The owl forgot its words: "Whooo, whooo... WHEEE!"
- The baby bat is fast asleep: "Zzz-squeak, zzz-squeak."

### 3. Action jokes

Three-quarters of children enjoyed bodily humour, such as strange walks, by 10 months. Start once your child stands with help: do the move, then invite them in.

- "Wiggle like a skeleton, from your toes up to your nose!"
- "Float like a sleepy ghost... and FLOP onto the cushion!"
- "Stir the potion round and round... oops, the spoon is on my head!"
- "Flap like a bat. Now flap like a bat that ate too much cake."
- "Stomp like a monster with BIG feet... now tiny mouse feet."
- "Freeze, you're a statue ghost! Unfreeze: wobble, wobble!"
- "Walk like a mummy, arms out, stiff legs... uh-oh, the mummy is ticklish!"

### 4. Wrong-name jokes

Deliberate mislabelling arrives later: half of children appreciated it by 29 months, three-quarters by 36. Point, look puzzled, and let your toddler shout the right name.

- Point at a pumpkin: "Look at that big orange... banana!"
- Hold a witch's hat: "My lovely new... shoe!" Then try it on your foot.
- Point at the black cat: "What a fluffy... cow! Moo? No? Meow!"
- Hold a toy spider: "My eight-legged... teddy bear."
- Pick up a broom: "Time for my... toothbrush!"
- Show a bat picture: "Here's a little flappy... fish!"
- Hold a wrapped sweet: "A shiny... telephone! Hello? Hello?"
- Point at an owl: "Who's in the tree? A big... duck! Quack-hoo!"

### 5. Finish-the-rhyme jokes

Nonsense words and mixed-up ideas reach half of children around 31 to 35 months. Stop before the last word and accept any answer, because a wrong rhyme is a joke too.

- "The little ghost said boo and lost its stripy... (shoe)!"
- "The pumpkin on the mat wore a pointy purple... (hat)!"
- "The black cat in the house is chasing one small... (mouse)!"
- "The bat up in the tree drank a cup of bedtime... (tea)!"
- "The witch flew on her broom round and round the... (room)!"
- "The spider on the bed wore socks of shiny... (red)!"
- "The skeleton in bed stood up on its... (head)!"

### 6. First knock-knock jokes for 4-year-olds

Nonsense knock-knocks sit in the survey's "playing with concepts" item, reached by three-quarters of children at 37 months, but puns stayed rare to 47 months. So these end in a sound, not a double meaning.

- Knock knock. Who's there? A ghost. A ghost who? A ghost who forgot to say boo!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Cat. Cat who? Cat-CHOO! Bless you, kitty!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Toad. Toad who? A toad in a tiny cape, ribbit!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Spider. Spider who? Spider-tickle, here it comes!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Moo. Moo who? A cow in a witch's hat!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Wobble. Wobble who? A jelly ghost going wobble, wobble!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Skeleton. Skeleton who? A skeleton with no tummy, so no cake for him!
- Knock knock. Who's there? Squeak. Squeak who? A little bat in squeaky shoes!

## Which Halloween joke fits which age in months?

Each row pairs an age band with the month by which half (or three-quarters) of children enjoyed that humour type in the 2021 survey. Children vary, so start there and adjust.

| Age (months) | Joke type | What to do | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6–12 (peekaboo: half by 1 month) | Peekaboo ghost | Hide behind a tea towel, reveal smiling | "Ghost eyes WIDE open!" |
| 12–24 (body humour: 75% by 10 months) | Silly sounds and actions | Exaggerate, then wait | "Rattle, rattle, BONK!" |
| 24–36 (wrong names: half by 29 months) | Wrong-name jokes | Point, mislabel, get corrected | "Big orange... banana!" |
| 30–42 (nonsense words: half by 35 months) | Finish-the-rhyme | Stop before the last word | "Lost its stripy... (shoe)!" |
| 42–48 (puns: under 25% by 47 months) | First knock-knocks | End on a sound or tickle | "Cat-CHOO! Bless you, kitty!" |

A two-year-old rarely gets a pun, and a four-year-old may find peekaboo babyish. Move up a row once your child starts correcting you.

## The never-scary rule for ages 1 to 4

Every joke here should end in a smile from a familiar face. The Early Humor Survey cites earlier work showing babies laugh when a parent plays peekaboo but are likelier to cry when a stranger does.

Toddlers do love scaring you: half were reported to enjoy "scaring others" by 16 months. Let them be the one who says boo, and keep your own reveals gentle.

- Hide behind a sheet or your hands, never a mask.
- Keep "boo" at talking volume and say "it's me" straight after.
- Skip monsters under the bed and anything that comes in the dark.
- Stop at the first wobbly lip and return to a joke that worked.

## Sending a toddler's Halloween jokes to someone far away

Faraway grandparents usually meet these jokes on a phone: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on one. A page can carry a costume photo and the favourite joke.

Our [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) has a kids tone that is spooky-cute: round blushing ghosts, no blood, no gore, no jump scares, and the trick becomes confetti spiders while nothing goes dark. It holds up to six photos and a letter, and the player wipes fog off portraits to reveal each photo, which plays like peekaboo.

Family mode changes the closing question to "Will you be my favourite little pumpkin?" For the joke in your toddler's own voice, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) takes a voice note of up to 60 seconds, and in its family and kids modes the No button never appears.

## When a Halloween joke, or our page, is the wrong choice

A screen is a poor stand-in for your face under 12 months, and every study cited here describes jokes told live by a familiar adult. Keep the page for a relative who cannot be in the room.

- **A tired or sensitive toddler:** skip Halloween jokes; plain peekaboo works any day.
- **A party or playgroup:** our page is a one-person greeting, not a group game or an invitation.
- **A grandparent who does not read English:** the page's interface is English only.
- **Same room on 31 October:** tell the joke live.

## Sources

- Hoicka E. et al., [The Early Humor Survey (EHS)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9374637), Behavior Research Methods, online 18 November 2021.
- Mireault G. et al., [Humour perception from 4 to 8 months](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6171116), British Journal of Developmental Psychology, 25 September 2017.
- Mireault G. and Reddy V., [Infants' differential responses to incongruity](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8291289), Human Development, 17 September 2020.
- Allison O., Kelsey C. and Grossmann T., [Social smiling and laughter in infants' default mode network](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12464472), Developmental Psychobiology, September 2025.
- SubhSandesh platform data, measured 24 September 2026.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The top five (Fatherly, The Scotsman, Mother&Baby, Kid Activities, WeAreTeachers) are general kids' lists with no age-in-months guidance, no table and no explanation of why toddlers laugh; this is the only page tying each joke type to the month children reach it (Early Humor Survey) with a never-scary rule, which is a concrete reason for an answer engine to cite it. It cannot overcome the incumbents' domain authority, the first-party numbers are platform-wide rather than Halloween data, and the SERP was measured once via WebSearch (US index), so expect months, not weeks.
